title: And can it be (Charles Wesley, 1738)
hook: my chains fell off, my heart was free
tomorrow: a hymn once titled 'Faith's Review and Expectation.' know it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, When I survey: Watts looked at the cross until the whole world seemed too small a gift. My soul, my life, my all. Today, another hymn, sung in the first person.
screen: `MY SOUL, MY LIFE, MY ALL.` → `SUNG IN THE FIRST PERSON.`

segments.voice: The last bell of the last exam. The cast cut off after six weeks. The day the debt is paid. Freedom has a feeling, and people describe it with their bodies: I could breathe, I felt light. So what does freedom feel like from the inside? Charles Wesley, John's brother, wrote a hymn that answers with a prison cell, and one line that ends in three short words: my chains fell off.
screen: `THE LAST BELL. THE CAST OFF.` → `WHAT DOES FREEDOM FEEL LIKE?` → `MY CHAINS FELL OFF.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. "Long my imprisoned spirit lay Fast bound in sin and nature's night; Thine eye diffused a quickening ray, I woke, the dungeon flamed with light; My chains fell off, my heart was free; I rose, went forth, and followed thee." Wesley is borrowing a scene from Acts. Peter sits chained in prison, an angel comes, "a light shined in the prison," and then: "his chains fell off from his hands." Wesley takes Peter's story and says me. My chains. My heart. That's the Christian answer: freedom from sin, through Christ, told as if you were in the cell. Now a neighbor who tells freedom the same way. At Passover, Jewish families retell the Exodus, the people of Israel brought out of slavery in Egypt. And the Mishnah teaches, in a paraphrase, that in every generation a person should see themselves as if they personally came out of Egypt. Not they. Me. That much is shared: an old rescue, told in the first person, so it happens again in the one telling it. And the honest difference. Passover remembers a whole people's freedom from real slavery, retold each year around a family table. Wesley's hymn sings one soul freed from sin by Christ's death, usually in church. Two ways of saying me, each in its own words.
screen: `THE DUNGEON FLAMED WITH LIGHT.` · `PETER'S CHAINS, IN ACTS.` · `PASSOVER: AS IF YOU CAME OUT.` · `A PEOPLE, OR ONE SOUL.` · then, large: `MY CHAINS FELL OFF.`

segments.voice: Name, silently, one chain that has fallen off in your life: a fear, a habit, a grudge, a long sickness. Then stand up and walk slowly across the room and back, the way the hymn ends: I rose, went forth. Sit down again and let your hands rest open.
And can it be. Charles Wesley's hymn of wonder, where Peter's prison becomes my prison, and the chains fall off me.
Your line: my chains fell off. An old rescue, sung as if it happened to the singer. Talk tomorrow.

chat.meaning: Shared: an old rescue told in the first person. Different: Passover remembers a people freed from slavery; the hymn sings one soul freed from sin by Christ.

Charles Wesley.meaning: an English hymn writer, brother of John Wesley

Passover.meaning: the Jewish festival retelling Israel's freedom from slavery in Egypt

Exodus.meaning: Israel's going out from Egypt; also the Bible book telling it

Mishnah.meaning: an early collection of Jewish oral law and teaching

quickening.meaning: old English: life-giving, bringing to life
